title: Which side of the plane should you sit on flying to Málaga?
author: Brogan
intro: Flying into Málaga, the left side of the plane is usually the better bet, with a view towards the city, its port and the Mediterranean as you come in to land. The right side gets the mountains and the resorts towards Torremolinos. Here's why, when it changes and which seats to pick.
seo_title: Flying to Málaga: which side of the plane to sit on
seo_description: Usually the left side (seat A) for Málaga city and the port as you land, the right for the mountains. Why the wind decides it and where to sit flying home.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Best side:** left, seat A
- **Why:** landings head south-east
- **Right side:** mountains and resorts
- **When it flips:** on some westerly winds

This is guidance, not a guarantee. The wind decides which way planes land, and air traffic control decides the exact route in, so no seat is certain. On most days, though, the left side faces the city.

sections.heading: Why the left side usually wins
sections.text:
Málaga's airport sits on the coast about 8 km south-west of the city centre, beside the mouth of the Guadalhorce river. It has two runways that run roughly north-west to south-east, and on most days planes land heading south-east, coming in from the north-west over the Guadalhorce valley and touching down with the sea just ahead.

On that final approach, Málaga city is off to your **left**, so from an A seat you may see the city spreading along the coast, the port and the hill of Gibralfaro above the old town. On the **right** side, you look towards the Sierra de Mijas and the Costa del Sol resorts of Torremolinos and Benalmádena.

Tip: before lining up, many flights from the UK come down over the sea or along the coast, so both sides may get a view of the Costa del Sol on the way in. Which side sees what then depends on the route you're given.

sections.heading: How the approach usually works
sections.text:
| Wind | Landing direction | Best side for the city |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Usual pattern | heading south-east, from over the valley | left (seat A) |
| Some westerly winds | heading north-west, in from the sea | right (seat F) |
| Light or changing winds | either | left is still the better bet |

When planes land the other way, they come in low over the sea and the coast near Torremolinos, and the city passes on the right instead. You won't know in advance, so book the left and take what comes.

sections.heading: Which seats to choose
sections.text:
Where you sit along the plane matters almost as much as the side:

- **In front of the wing** gives the clearest view, but those rows often cost more to choose.
- **Behind the wing** is usually the best value, with a clear view down as the plane descends.
- **Over the wing**, the wing and engine block most of the view below.
- **Check the seat map:** some window seats on popular jets don't line up with a window at all.

On a Boeing 737 or Airbus A320, which most airlines use for Málaga, the left window seat is **A** and the right is **F**. If your airline assigns seats for free at check-in, paying to choose is the only way to be sure of a left-side window.

sections.heading: On the way home
sections.text:
Most departures take off towards the south-east, out over the sea, and then turn back north for the UK. Which side gets the best view depends on the turn, so it varies from flight to flight, but you'll often see the coast and the city on the climb out.

Watch out: on afternoon flights home, the sun is often on the left side of the plane heading north, so a right-hand seat can be more comfortable if you'd rather read or sleep.

The flight from the UK takes about two and three-quarter hours from London, and a little over three hours from the north of England and Scotland.

sections.heading: What you might see
sections.text:
On a clear day, coming in to land you might spot:

- **Málaga city**, with the port, the cathedral and the Alcazaba and Gibralfaro castle on the hill.
- **The Guadalhorce valley**, a patchwork of farms and orchards running inland.
- **The Sierra de Mijas**, the mountains behind Torremolinos, Benalmádena and Mijas.
- **The Costa del Sol**, with its beaches and resorts stretching west towards Marbella.

On a very clear winter day, the high peaks of the Sierra Nevada, far to the east behind Granada, can sometimes be seen with snow on them.

sections.text:

faqs.question: Which side of the plane is best for landing at Málaga?
faqs.answer: Usually the left side, seat A on most short-haul jets. On most days planes land heading south-east, and the city and port are on the left. The right side looks towards the mountains and Torremolinos.

faqs.question: Do planes land over the sea at Málaga?
faqs.answer: Not usually. On most days they come in from the north-west over the Guadalhorce valley and land towards the sea. On some days with westerly winds they land the other way, in from the sea.

faqs.question: How long is the flight to Málaga from the UK?
faqs.answer: About two and three-quarter hours from London, and a little over three hours from northern England and Scotland.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying to choose a window seat to Málaga?
faqs.answer: Only if the view matters to you. It's a lovely approach on a clear day, but the flight is short, and a free seat at check-in may land you on either side.
